Amazon DynamoDB

Build serverless NoSQL applications with Amazon DynamoDB: keys, capacity, indexes, global tables, DAX, backups, and cost.

Overview and Objectives

Lesson Overview

AWS Database Services

AWS offers a purpose-built database service for each kind of data. This lesson covers Amazon DynamoDB, the serverless key-value and document database.

DynamoDB trades joins and ad hoc SQL for predictable performance at any scale and no servers to manage. This lesson shows how items and keys work, how to set the capacity and the table class, how indexes, consistency, and transactions shape the queries, how global tables, DAX, Streams, and TTL extend a table, how backups and exports protect the data, and what DynamoDB costs. It ends with a comparison of the options. The last two tabs prepare you for the AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate (SAA-C03) exam.

The tabs in this lesson cover the following topics:

  • Tab 1: tables, items, primary keys, Query and Scan, and when to use DynamoDB.
  • Tab 2: provisioned and on-demand capacity, capacity units, and table classes.
  • Tab 3: global and local secondary indexes, read consistency, and transactions.
  • Tab 4: global tables, DynamoDB Accelerator, Streams, and Time to Live.
  • Tab 5: point-in-time recovery, on-demand backups, export to S3, and security.
  • Tab 6: what you pay for, and how to lower the cost.
  • Tab 7: comparison tables and the SAA-C03 cheat sheet with decision rules.
  • Tab 8: open-ended Knowledge Check questions with model answers.

Introduction

A relational database is the right tool when the data needs joins and ad hoc queries. Many modern applications instead read and write by a known key, need a flexible item shape, and need the same speed at any size. DynamoDB is built for that workload. An architect must know how to model the keys, how to choose the capacity mode, and which feature solves which scaling or resilience need.

This lesson assumes that you know the database types from Lesson 272.1 and the Aurora Global Database from Lesson 272.2. It follows FlashCart Inc. through the Problem Statement of each tab.

Use the tab list on the left, or the Previous and Next buttons, to move through the lesson. Each topic tab opens with a Problem Statement and ends with exam traps, keyword triggers, and resource links. The Knowledge Check is the last tab.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, learners will be able to:

  1. Define Amazon DynamoDB, and describe its tables, items, attributes, and primary keys.
  2. Differentiate Query from Scan, and explain the 400 KB item limit.
  3. Compare provisioned and on-demand capacity modes, and calculate capacity units.
  4. Choose between a global secondary index and a local secondary index, and select a read consistency.
  5. Explain global tables, DAX, DynamoDB Streams, and TTL.
  6. Select a backup, restore, or export method for a DynamoDB table.
  7. Design a DynamoDB solution for a global application with performance and cost requirements.
  8. Determine cost-effective AWS database services for a workload, for example DynamoDB compared with Amazon RDS, and serverless options.

1. What Amazon DynamoDB Is

Problem Statement

FlashCart keeps its shopping carts and sessions in a relational database. During the sale the table is hot, schema changes are slow, and the team spends time on capacity. The engineers want a store with single-digit millisecond reads and writes at any scale, a flexible item shape, and no servers to manage.

1.1 What Amazon DynamoDB Is

  • Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed, serverless NoSQL database for key-value and document data.
  • It gives consistent single-digit millisecond reads and writes at any scale, with millions of requests per second and hundreds of terabytes of data.
  • There are no servers to provision or patch. Data is stored across multiple Availability Zones by default, and data at rest is always encrypted.
  • Global tables add multi-Region replication with up to 99.999 percent availability.
  • It is an AWS proprietary technology, with no joins between tables and no SQL engine for ad hoc analysis.
  • It is integrated with IAM for security, authorization, and administration, and it has low-cost, automatic scaling.

1.2 Tables, Items, and Attributes

  • A table is the basic entity. It holds items, which are like rows, and each item has attributes.
  • The primary key must be decided when you create the table. A table can hold an unlimited number of items.
  • The primary key identifies each item. It is either a partition key alone, or a partition key plus a sort key.
  • DynamoDB uses the partition key to decide where an item is stored, so a good key spreads the requests evenly.
  • Attributes can be scalars (string, number, binary, Boolean), documents (maps and lists in JSON style), or sets.
  • Items in one table can have different attributes. There is no fixed schema, apart from the key. You can add attributes over time, and an attribute can be null.
  • The data types are: scalar (string, number, binary, Boolean, and null), document (list and map), and set (string set, number set, and binary set).
  • The maximum item size is 400 KB, including attribute names and values. Store a large object in Amazon S3 and keep its location in the item.

1.3 Supported Data Types

  • DynamoDB groups its data types into three categories: scalar types, document types, and set types.
  • When you create a table or a secondary index, you must give the name and the data type of each primary key attribute. A key attribute must be a string, a number, or binary.
  • DynamoDB is schemaless. Apart from the primary key attributes, you do not define any attributes or data types when you create a table. A relational database needs the name and the data type of every column when you create a table.
CategoryTypeWhat it holds and the main rules
ScalarNumberPositive, negative, or zero, with up to 38 digits of precision. Use a string for more precision. DynamoDB sends numbers over the network as strings, but treats them as numbers for math.
ScalarStringUnicode text in UTF-8. The length can be zero if the attribute is not a key. A partition key can be up to 2048 bytes, and a sort key up to 1024 bytes.
ScalarBinaryAny binary data, such as compressed text, encrypted data, or images. The application encodes the value in base64 before it sends it. The same key length limits apply.
ScalarBooleantrue or false.
ScalarNullAn attribute with an unknown or undefined state.
DocumentListAn ordered collection of values in square brackets, like a JSON array. The elements can be of different types.
DocumentMapAn unordered collection of name-value pairs in curly braces, like a JSON object. Maps are ideal for storing JSON documents.
SetString set, number set, and binary setSeveral unique values of the same type. The order is not preserved. DynamoDB does not support an empty set.
  • Lists and maps can be nested inside each other, up to 32 levels deep. There is no limit on the number of values in a list, a map, or a set, as long as the item stays within the 400 KB item size limit.
  • An empty string or an empty binary value is allowed if the attribute is not a key. Empty lists and empty maps are allowed.
  • DynamoDB has no native date and time type. Store a date as a string in ISO 8601 format, which people can read, or as a number in Unix epoch seconds, which uses less storage and works with TTL.

Examples of a list, a map, and the three kinds of sets:

FavoriteThings: ["Cookies", "Coffee", 3.14159]

{
    Day: "Monday",
    UnreadEmails: 42,
    ItemsOnMyDesk: [
        "Coffee Cup",
        "Telephone",
        { Pens: { Quantity : 3 }, Pencils: { Quantity : 2 } }
    ]
}

["Black", "Green", "Red"]
[42.2, -19, 7.5, 3.14]
["U3Vubnk=", "UmFpbnk=", "U25vd3k="]

1.4 Data Type Descriptors

The low-level DynamoDB API uses short tokens, called data type descriptors, to tell DynamoDB how to interpret each attribute. The query command in 1.6 uses "N" for a number.

DescriptorTypeDescriptorType
SStringMMap
NNumberLList
BBinarySSString set
BOOLBooleanNSNumber set
NULLNullBSBinary set

1.5 Naming Rules

  • All names are encoded in UTF-8 and are case-sensitive.
  • Table names and index names must be between 3 and 255 characters long. They can contain only the letters a to z and A to Z, the digits 0 to 9, an underscore (_), a dash (-), and a dot (.).
  • Attribute names must be at least one character long and less than 64 KB. The names of secondary index partition keys and sort keys, and of the projected attributes of a local secondary index, must be no longer than 255 characters.
  • Keep attribute names short. Attribute names are counted in the storage and in the throughput that DynamoDB meters, so short names lower the read request units that you use.
  • DynamoDB has a list of reserved words, and the characters # (hash) and : (colon) have a special meaning. You can use them in names, but you should avoid them, because you must then define placeholder names in every expression.
  • Choose names that are meaningful and concise, such as Products, Books, and Authors.

1.6 Query and Scan

QueryScan
What it readsItems that match a partition key, with optional conditions on the sort key.Every item in the table or index.
Speed and costFast and efficient. It looks only in the matching partition.Slow and expensive on large tables.
FiltersA filter runs after the read, so it saves bandwidth but not read capacity.A filter narrows the result, but DynamoDB still reads all the items first.

Examples with the AWS CLI, for an Orders table that has the partition key UserId:

aws dynamodb query \
  --table-name Orders \
  --key-condition-expression "UserId = :userid" \
  --expression-attribute-values '{":userid":{"N":"103"}}'

aws dynamodb scan \
  --table-name Orders \
  --filter-expression "Product = :name" \
  --expression-attribute-values '{":name":{"S":"Widget"}}'

1.7 When to Use DynamoDB

  • Predictable access patterns, where about 90 to 95 percent of the queries are known in advance.
  • Workloads that need steady performance at any scale, such as shopping carts, sessions, user profiles, leaderboards, and IoT data.
  • A flexible item shape, for example a product catalog or a game.
  • Not a fit: ad hoc queries with joins, and complex analytics. Use a relational database or export the data to Amazon S3 for analysis.

1.7.1 Real-World Scenario: Shopping Carts During a Flash Sale

The situation. FlashCart runs a flash sale four times a year. On a normal day, about 5,000 shoppers use the site at the same time. When a sale starts at 10:00, traffic jumps to about 300,000 shoppers within minutes, and every one of them adds items to a cart. Carts were stored in the relational order database, which slowed down and timed out at the start of the last sale, and blocked checkout too.

Why DynamoDB fits.

  • Known access patterns: the app always reads and writes the cart of one customer, so every request is a lookup by key. No joins and no ad hoc queries are needed.
  • Scale and spikes: in on-demand capacity mode, DynamoDB serves the jump from 5,000 to 300,000 shoppers without capacity planning, and FlashCart pays per request, so quiet days cost little.
  • Steady latency: reads and writes stay in single-digit milliseconds, whether 100 or 100,000 shoppers use the table.
  • Automatic cleanup: TTL deletes abandoned carts after 7 days, at no extra write cost.
  • No servers to manage: there is no database instance to size, patch, or fail over, and the data is replicated across Availability Zones by default.
  • Decoupled checkout: DynamoDB Streams send cart changes to a Lambda function (lesson 273.1), so the order system is updated without slowing the shopper down.

Table design.

AttributeRoleExample
customerIdPartition key: spreads the carts across partitions.C-10482
skSort key: one item per product in the cart.ITEM#P-2291
quantity, price, addedAtOrdinary attributes.2, 24.99, 2026-11-27T10:01:12Z
expiresAtTTL attribute, in Unix epoch seconds, 7 days after the last change.1797415272
 
{
  "customerId": "C-10482",
  "sk": "ITEM#P-2291",
  "quantity": 2,
  "price": 24.99,
  "addedAt": "2026-11-27T10:01:12Z",
  "expiresAt": 1797415272
}
Access patternDynamoDB operation
Show the cart of a customerQuery on customerId
Add or change one product in the cartPutItem or UpdateItem on customerId and sk
Remove one productDeleteItem on customerId and sk
Empty the cart after checkoutBatchWriteItem or a transaction with the order write

Where DynamoDB would not fit in the same company. The finance team wants a monthly report of sales by region, product category, and discount, joined with returns. That is an ad hoc, analytical query across many items, so FlashCart exports the data to Amazon S3 and queries it with Athena (lesson 272.11), or loads it into Redshift (lesson 272.8). The order records themselves, which need joins with payments and invoices, stay in Aurora.

1.8 SQL or NoSQL?

QuestionPoints to SQLPoints to NoSQL (DynamoDB)
Do you need to run ad hoc queries?Yes.No.
Are 90 to 95 percent of the queries defined in advance?No.Yes.
Is the traffic predictable?Yes, in most cases.Not necessarily. DynamoDB also handles spikes.
Do you need consistent performance at any scale?Not as a main need.Yes.
Is the schema mostly fixed, or flexible?Mostly fixed.Flexible.
ExampleA flight booking system, and banking. The databases are Oracle, SQL Server, Aurora, PostgreSQL, and MySQL.An e-commerce product catalog, and multiplayer games. The databases are MongoDB, Cassandra, and DynamoDB.

Instead of one relational database for every need, AWS offers purpose-built databases. Each type fits a kind of data and a kind of workload.

Database typeTypical workloadsAWS services

1.10 Relational Databases, Aurora, and DynamoDB Compared

CharacteristicRelational database management system (RDBMS)Amazon DynamoDB
Optimal workloadsAd hoc queries, data warehousing, and online analytical processing (OLAP).Web-scale applications, such as social networks, gaming, media sharing, and Internet of Things (IoT).
Data modelA well-defined schema: data is normalized into tables, rows, and columns, and the relationships are defined among tables, columns, and indexes.Schemaless. Every table needs a primary key, and there are no constraints on the other attributes. It can manage structured or semistructured data, including JSON documents.
Data accessSQL is the standard, and all the tools use SQL.The AWS Management Console, the AWS CLI, NoSQL Workbench, PartiQL (a SQL-compatible language), and the AWS SDKs.
PerformanceOptimized for storage, so it depends on the disk subsystem. Developers and administrators optimize queries, indexes, and table structures.Optimized for compute, so it depends mainly on the hardware and the network latency. As a managed service, DynamoDB hides these details.
ScalingEasiest to scale up with faster hardware. Spreading tables over several hosts needs more investment, and there are maximum sizes.Designed to scale out on distributed clusters. Throughput grows without more latency, and there is no upper limit on the items per table or the table size.

Amazon Aurora is a relational database, so it keeps the relational model. The following table compares it with DynamoDB:

Amazon AuroraAmazon DynamoDB
Data modelRelational tables that you query with SQL, with joins.Key-value and document items, with no joins.
SchemaDefined columns and data types.Only the primary key is defined.
QueriesAd hoc SQL queries.Queries by key, with secondary indexes. Plan the access patterns first.
TransactionsACID transactions.Transactions across items in one Region and one account.
ScalingOne writer and up to 15 replicas, with storage up to 128 TiB, or 256 TiB on recent engine versions. Serverless v2 adjusts the capacity.Scales out with no servers to manage, and no limit on the table size.
Multi-RegionAurora Global Database: one writer Region.Global tables: every Region accepts writes.
Cost modelInstance hours or ACU-hours, storage, and I/O.Read and write requests or capacity, and storage.
Choose it whenThe workload needs joins, ad hoc queries, or complex transactions, or the application already uses MySQL or PostgreSQL.The access patterns are known, and the workload needs steady millisecond performance at any scale.

1.12 Exam-Style Question

Written for this course.

Scenario: A company needs a database for user sessions. It needs single-digit millisecond reads and writes at any scale, no servers to manage, and a flexible item structure. Which solution meets the requirements?

  • A. Amazon DynamoDB.
  • B. Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with a large instance.
  • C. Amazon Redshift.
  • D. Amazon EBS volumes with a custom database.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: A. DynamoDB is a serverless NoSQL database with millisecond performance at any scale and a flexible item structure.

OptionResultReason
ACorrectIt matches every requirement with no servers to manage.
BIncorrectRDS needs instance sizing, and a fixed schema is the norm.
CIncorrectRedshift is a data warehouse for analytics, not for session lookups.
DIncorrectA custom database on EBS means managing servers.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • The primary key is a partition key, or a partition key plus a sort key. The two together must be unique.
  • An item can be at most 400 KB. For larger data, store the object in S3 and the pointer in DynamoDB.
  • Query uses the key and is efficient. Scan reads everything, and a filter does not reduce what a scan reads.
  • DynamoDB has no native date and time type. Use an ISO 8601 string or an epoch number, and an epoch number in seconds for TTL.
  • A set holds unique values of one type and cannot be empty. A list is ordered and a map is unordered.

Memory Hook

Partition key places it. Sort key orders it. Query is cheap. Scan is costly.

→ Amazon DynamoDB

Trigger 2: "Retrieve items by key without reading the whole table"
→ Query

Trigger 3: "Item larger than 400 KB"
→ Store the object in Amazon S3 and keep a pointer in DynamoDB

2. Capacity Modes and Table Classes

Problem Statement

Every night the FlashCart load is small, but on Friday at 09:00 the traffic jumps by tenfold. A table that was sized for the peak wastes money all week, and a table that was sized for the average throttles on Friday. The team has to choose how to set the capacity, and how to lower the storage cost of old order history.

2.1 Read and Write Capacity

  • DynamoDB has two capacity modes: provisioned (the default) and on-demand.
  • You can switch from provisioned to on-demand up to four times in a 24-hour period, and from on-demand to provisioned at any time.
Provisioned capacity modeOn-demand capacity mode
How it worksYou set the read capacity units (RCUs) and the write capacity units (WCUs) for the table. You can add auto scaling.No capacity to set. DynamoDB scales automatically, and you pay per request.
Best forPredictable or steady traffic.Unpredictable or spiky traffic, and new tables with an unknown load.
CostCheaper when the workload is steady.Costlier per request for steady high throughput.
ThrottlingPossible when the traffic goes above the capacity.Virtually none for the traffic that it can serve.

2.2 Capacity Units

UnitWhat it gives
1 read capacity unit (RCU)One strongly consistent read per second, or two eventually consistent reads per second, for an item up to 4 KB.
Transactional readNeeds 2 RCUs per read per second for an item up to 4 KB.
1 write capacity unit (WCU)One write per second for an item up to 1 KB.
  • DynamoDB rounds up to the next unit. A strongly consistent read of a 10 KB item takes 3 RCUs, and a transactional read of the same item takes 6.
  • On-demand tables use read request units and write request units of the same sizes.
  • When the traffic goes above the provisioned capacity, DynamoDB throttles the requests. Use auto scaling, or retry with a backoff.

2.3 Table Classes

DynamoDB Standard (default)DynamoDB Standard-IA
Storage costHigher.Lower.
Read and write costLower.Higher.
Best forFrequently accessed tables.Tables where storage is the largest cost, such as history, archives, and old sessions.
  • You can change the table class of a table in either direction.
  • Standard-IA works with global tables, point-in-time recovery, streams, TTL, transactions, and DAX.

2.4 Partition Key Design and Hot Partitions

  • DynamoDB hashes the partition key of each item to choose the partition where the item is stored. Each partition is designed to deliver up to 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second.
  • A hot partition receives much more traffic than the others, for example because one key value is very popular. It is throttled at the partition limit, even when the table as a whole still has unused capacity. A throttled request returns ProvisionedThroughputExceededException, and the AWS SDKs retry it with exponential backoff.
  • Design for uniform activity: choose a partition key with many distinct values (high cardinality) that requests use evenly, such as customerId or orderId. Avoid keys with few values or a time-based key that sends all of today’s writes to one value, such as status = "active" or date = "2026-11-27".
  • Write sharding spreads the writes for one popular value over several partition keys by adding a suffix, for example "2026-11-27#1" to "2026-11-27#10". Readers query all the shards and merge the results.
  • Burst capacity: DynamoDB keeps up to 5 minutes (300 seconds) of unused read and write capacity, which absorbs short spikes. DynamoDB can also use burst capacity for background maintenance, so do not plan on it.
  • Adaptive capacity: DynamoDB automatically gives more throughput to a busy partition, and it can isolate a frequently accessed item on its own partition. It is enabled for every table at no extra cost, in both on-demand and provisioned modes, but it cannot raise one partition key above the partition limit.
  • For read-heavy hot keys, such as a product on the home page, put DAX or another cache in front of the table.
Partition keyGood choice?Why
customerIdYesMany distinct values, and requests are spread across customers.
orderStatus ("active", "shipped")NoFew values, so most requests hit one or two partitions.
orderDate (one value per day)NoAll the writes of the day go to the same key.
orderDate plus a shard suffix (#1 to #10)Yes, for writesWrite sharding spreads the daily writes over 10 keys.

2.5 Exam-Style Question

Written for this course.

Scenario: A company stores seven years of order history in DynamoDB. The data is read rarely, and storage is the largest part of the cost. The company wants to lower the cost without changing the application. Which solution meets the requirements?

  • A. Change the table class to DynamoDB Standard-IA.
  • B. Switch the table to on-demand mode.
  • C. Add a DAX cluster.
  • D. Create a global secondary index on every attribute.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: A. Standard-IA has a lower storage price and a higher request price, so it fits a table that is large and rarely read. It needs no application change.

OptionResultReason
ACorrectIt lowers the dominant storage cost.
BIncorrectOn-demand mode changes how requests are billed, not the storage price.
CIncorrectDAX adds a cache cost and helps repeated reads.
DIncorrectIndexes copy data and raise the storage cost.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • 1 RCU = one strongly consistent read of 4 KB per second, or two eventually consistent reads. 1 WCU = one write of 1 KB per second.
  • Provisioned is cheaper for steady traffic and can throttle. On-demand fits spikes and costs more per request.
  • Standard-IA = lower storage cost and higher request cost.
  • A table can throttle even with unused capacity, because of a hot partition: one partition is limited to 3,000 RCUs and 1,000 WCUs. The fix is a high-cardinality partition key or write sharding, not more table capacity.

Memory Hook

Steady = provisioned. Spiky or unknown = on-demand. Cold and big = Standard-IA.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "Unpredictable or spiky traffic with no capacity planning"
→ On-demand capacity mode

Trigger 2: "Steady traffic at the lowest cost"
→ Provisioned capacity with auto scaling

Trigger 3: "Rarely accessed data where storage is the main cost"
→ DynamoDB Standard-IA table class

Trigger 4: "Throttling on one popular key while the table has spare capacity"
→ Hot partition: redesign the key or shard the writes

Trigger 5: "Many reads of the same few items"
→ DAX in front of the table

3. Indexes, Consistency, and Transactions

Problem Statement

The FlashCart orders table is keyed by customer, so it answers the question "show the orders of customer 103" quickly. Now the support team asks "show all the orders for one product" and "show the latest order of any customer". Also, a payment and an inventory update must succeed together or not at all.

3.1 Secondary Indexes

Global secondary index (GSI)Local secondary index (LSI)
KeysA different partition key and an optional sort key.The same partition key as the table, with a different sort key.
When you create itAt any time.Only when you create the table.
ConsistencyEventually consistent only.Eventually or strongly consistent.
CapacityHas its own read and write capacity in provisioned mode.Uses the capacity of the base table.
Use it forA new access pattern that the primary key cannot support.Another sort order inside the same partition key.
  • A GSI keeps a copy of the attributes that you project into it, and DynamoDB updates it automatically when the table changes.
  • Example: an Orders table is keyed by customer, and it answers "show the orders of one customer". A GSI with the order date as the sort key answers "what is the most recent order?" in a different way, without a scan.
  • Example: a GameScores table is keyed by user and game title. A GSI keyed by game title, with the top score as the sort key, answers "what is the top score ever recorded for the game Meteor Blasters?".
  • A table can have up to 20 GSIs by default.

3.2 Read Consistency

  • Eventually consistent reads (the default) may not show a write that just finished. They cost half as much.
  • Strongly consistent reads return the latest data. Set the consistent read option on the request. They are not available on a GSI.
  • Transactional reads give an all-or-nothing view of several items, and cost twice as much as a strongly consistent read.

3.3 Transactions

  • DynamoDB transactions give ACID (atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability) across one or more tables in one account and one Region.
  • Use them when several writes must succeed or fail together, for example a payment and an inventory change.
  • Transactions are not supported across Regions in global tables.
  • A transactional operation uses more capacity than a normal one.

3.4 Conditional Writes and Optimistic Locking

  • By default, a write replaces or changes an item no matter what is in it. A conditional write succeeds only if the item meets a condition that you give in a ConditionExpression. It works with PutItem, UpdateItem, and DeleteItem.
  • If the condition is false, the write fails with ConditionalCheckFailedException, and nothing changes.
  • Use it to stop a lost update or a double action, for example to create an item only if it does not exist yet, or to sell an item only if stock is greater than zero.
  • Optimistic locking adds a version number attribute to the item. A client reads the item and its version, and writes only if the version is still the same, adding 1 to it. If another client changed the item in between, the write fails, and the client reads it again and retries.
  • An atomic counter, such as a page view count, uses UpdateItem with ADD to increase a number without reading it first.
aws dynamodb update-item \
  --table-name Inventory \
  --key '{"productId": {"S": "P-2291"}}' \
  --update-expression "SET stock = stock - :one, version = version + :one" \
  --condition-expression "stock > :zero AND version = :v" \
  --expression-attribute-values '{":one":{"N":"1"}, ":zero":{"N":"0"}, ":v":{"N":"7"}}'

This write sells one unit of product P-2291 only if stock is still above zero and the item is still at version 7. If two shoppers try to buy the last unit at the same time, only one write succeeds.

3.5 Hands-On Lab

Hands-On Lab

3.6 Exam-Style Question

Written for this course.

Scenario: A DynamoDB table is keyed by CustomerId and OrderDate. The application must now also look up orders by ProductId, and the lookup does not use CustomerId. Which solution meets the requirements?

  • A. Create a global secondary index with ProductId as the partition key.
  • B. Create a local secondary index with ProductId as the partition key.
  • C. Run a scan with a filter on ProductId.
  • D. Create a second table with the same data and copy the changes by hand.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: A. A GSI can use a different partition key and can be added to an existing table, so it supports the new access pattern efficiently.

OptionResultReason
ACorrectA GSI answers a query on another key.
BIncorrectAn LSI must keep the table partition key and can only be created with the table.
CIncorrectA scan reads every item, which is slow and costly.
DIncorrectA manual copy adds work and risks stale data.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • A GSI can be added any time and has a different partition key. An LSI is created with the table and keeps the table partition key.
  • A GSI supports eventually consistent reads only.
  • A transaction works inside one Region. It is not supported across Regions in global tables.
  • Two clients overwrite each other’s changes = lost update. The fix is a conditional write with a version attribute (optimistic locking), not a stronger read consistency.

Memory Hook

GSI = a new key, any time. LSI = a new sort order, at creation.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "Query by an attribute that is not the primary key"
→ A global secondary index

Trigger 2: "Several writes must all succeed or all fail"
→ DynamoDB transactions

Trigger 3: "The newest data on every read"
→ A strongly consistent read

Trigger 4: "Prevent two users from overwriting the same item"
→ Conditional write with optimistic locking

Trigger 5: "Create the item only if it does not exist"
→ PutItem with attribute_not_exists in a ConditionExpression

4. Global Tables, DAX, Streams, and TTL

Problem Statement

FlashCart now sells in Europe and Asia. Customers in London and Mumbai see slow responses when the table is only in Virginia, and a Regional outage would stop the whole shop. Product pages also repeat the same reads many times, and the warehouse wants a message every time an order changes. Old sessions should disappear by themselves.

4.1 Global Tables

  • A global table is a multi-Region, multi-active, serverless table. You can read and write in any replica, and DynamoDB copies the changes to the others.
  • It gives low-latency access for users around the world, and it survives the failure of a whole Region. Availability reaches up to 99.999 percent.
  • By default, global tables use multi-Region eventual consistency, and when two Regions write the same item, the last writer wins.
  • Global tables also offer multi-Region strong consistency, for applications that need zero data loss across Regions.
  • Transactions are not supported across Regions in global tables.
  • DynamoDB Streams are a prerequisite of a global table, because DynamoDB uses them to replicate the changes (course slide).

4.2 DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)

  • DAX is a fully managed, highly available, in-memory cache for DynamoDB. It brings read latency down from milliseconds to microseconds.
  • It is API-compatible with DynamoDB. Only the client and the endpoint change in an existing application.
  • DAX serves eventually consistent reads. It is not for strongly consistent reads, write-heavy workloads, or workloads without repeated reads.
  • Use a cluster with several nodes across Availability Zones for production.
  • DAX gives up to a 10 times improvement in read performance. The default time to live of its cache is 5 minutes.
  • Typical uses: real-time bidding, social gaming, and trading applications.

4.3 DynamoDB Streams

  • A stream captures item-level changes in a time-ordered sequence, and keeps them for 24 hours.
  • It works asynchronously, so it does not slow the table. You can turn it on for a new or an existing table.
  • Use it to trigger Lambda functions, send notifications through SNS (lesson 273.3), feed Kinesis (lesson 273.6), or copy the changes to another store.
  • Typical uses: react to changes in real time, such as a welcome email to a new user; real-time monitoring of connected vehicles and sensors; real-time usage analytics; inserting into derivative tables; and cross-Region replication.
DynamoDB StreamsKinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB
Retention24 hours.Up to 1 year.
ConsumersA limited number.A high number.

4.4 Time to Live (TTL)

  • TTL deletes expired items automatically. You choose a numeric attribute that holds an expiry time in Unix epoch seconds.
  • DynamoDB removes expired items in the background. A deletion by TTL uses no write capacity and has no extra charge.
  • Expired items may still appear for a short time before the background process removes them.
  • Typical uses: user sessions and tokens, which are removed when they expire; rate-limiting counters, such as the number of API hits per minute, which reset by TTL; OTP and verification codes; temporary data and old logs; and keeping only current items to meet regulatory obligations.
  • The expiry attribute holds an epoch time in seconds. A background process scans the table and deletes the items whose expiry time is before the current time.

4.5 Exam-Style Question

Written for this course.

Scenario: A company runs a shopping site on DynamoDB. The product table gets the same reads again and again, and the company wants microsecond read latency with very few code changes. Which solution meets the requirements?

  • A. Add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the table.
  • B. Switch the table to on-demand mode.
  • C. Add a global secondary index.
  • D. Add Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: A. DAX is a DynamoDB-compatible in-memory cache that serves repeated reads in microseconds, and the application only changes its client and endpoint.

OptionResultReason
ACorrectDAX is purpose-built for read-heavy DynamoDB tables.
BIncorrectThe capacity mode does not change the read latency.
CIncorrectA GSI supports another query pattern, not faster repeated reads.
DIncorrectS3 Transfer Acceleration is for S3 uploads.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • Global tables = active-active, multi-Region writes. Aurora Global Database has one writer Region.
  • DAX is only for DynamoDB and eventually consistent reads. If the source is RDS or Aurora, or the question asks for advanced data structures, the answer is ElastiCache.
  • Streams keep changes for 24 hours. TTL deletes expired items at no write cost.

Memory Hook

Global tables = write anywhere. DAX = microsecond reads. Streams = change feed. TTL = free cleanup.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "Active-active database in several Regions with low latency for users everywhere"
→ DynamoDB global tables

Trigger 2: "Microsecond reads for a DynamoDB table with no major code changes"
→ DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)

Trigger 3: "React to every change of an item"
→ DynamoDB Streams with Lambda

Trigger 4: "Delete expired session items automatically"
→ DynamoDB TTL

5. Backup, Export, and Security

Problem Statement

An engineer deleted the wrong items from the FlashCart sessions table. The team needs to bring the table back to a minute before the mistake, keep monthly backups for audits, and let the analysts query last quarter data without slowing the live table. The security team also asks how the table is protected.

5.1 Backup and Restore

Point-in-time recovery (PITR)On-demand backup
What it isContinuous backups of the table.A full manual snapshot that you start.
RetentionA recovery period of 1 to 35 days that you choose.Kept until you delete it.
Restore toAny second inside the recovery period.The time of the backup.
  • A restore always creates a new table.
  • You can use AWS Backup to schedule backups and to copy them to another Region or account.
  • Backups do not use the read and write capacity of the table.

5.2 Export to S3 and Import From S3

  • Export to S3 writes the table data to Amazon S3 from a point in time, and it needs PITR to be on. It does not use read capacity. Use it for analytics with Athena, pipelines, and long-term storage.
  • Import from S3 loads CSV, DynamoDB JSON, or Amazon Ion files into a new table. It does not use write capacity, and it cannot overwrite an existing table. Import errors are logged in Amazon CloudWatch Logs (lesson 274.2).
  • An export works for any point in time in the last 35 days, and it writes DynamoDB JSON or Ion files. Use it to analyze the data with Athena, to keep snapshots for auditing, and to run ETL on the data before you import it back.

5.3 Security

  • Encryption at rest is always on, with AWS KMS keys. Encryption in transit uses HTTPS.
  • IAM policies control who can use a table, down to the item and attribute level with condition keys. Resource-based policies are available for tables and streams.
  • A VPC endpoint keeps the traffic between your VPC and DynamoDB on the AWS network.
  • AWS CloudTrail (lesson 274.3) records the API calls, and CloudWatch (lesson 274.1) has the metrics and alarms.
  • DynamoDB tables cannot be made public, because Block Public Access is always on.

5.4 Private Access From a VPC

  • DynamoDB is a public AWS service endpoint. By default, an EC2 instance or a Lambda function in a private subnet reaches it through a NAT gateway and the internet.
  • A gateway VPC endpoint for DynamoDB adds a route to the route tables of your subnets, so the traffic to DynamoDB stays on the AWS network, with no NAT gateway, internet gateway, or public IP address needed.
  • Gateway endpoints are available only for DynamoDB and Amazon S3, and they have no hourly charge. Using one also saves the NAT gateway data processing charges for the DynamoDB traffic.
  • An endpoint policy can limit which tables and actions the endpoint allows, and a policy on the table side can require that requests come through a specific endpoint, with the aws:SourceVpce condition.
  • DynamoDB also supports interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink), which have private IP addresses and can be reached from on-premises networks through AWS Direct Connect or a VPN. Interface endpoints are charged per hour and per GB.

5.5 Fine-Grained Access Control

  • IAM policies can limit access not only to a table but to specific items and attributes, with IAM condition keys.
  • dynamodb:LeadingKeys limits a user to the items whose partition key matches a value, such as the user’s own ID. dynamodb:Attributes limits which attributes a user can read or write.
  • A common pattern is a mobile app with Cognito (lesson 273.2) identity pools: each user gets temporary credentials, and the policy uses the user’s Cognito identity ID as the leading key, so each user can only read and write their own items.
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": ["dynamodb:GetItem", "dynamodb:PutItem", "dynamodb:UpdateItem", "dynamodb:Query"],
  "Resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:us-east-1:111122223333:table/Carts",
  "Condition": {
    "ForAllValues:StringEquals": {
      "dynamodb:LeadingKeys": ["${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}"]
    }
  }
}

5.7 Exam-Style Question

Written for this course.

Scenario: A DynamoDB table was changed by mistake 20 minutes ago. The company needs the table as it was 30 minutes ago, and it has point-in-time recovery turned on. Which solution meets the requirements?

  • A. Restore the table to a point in time, which creates a new table.
  • B. Restore the table over the existing one.
  • C. Replay the DynamoDB stream from last week.
  • D. Switch the table to on-demand mode.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: A. PITR restores to any second inside the recovery period, and it always creates a new table. The team then switches the application to it.

OptionResultReason
ACorrectA point-in-time restore gives the table as of the chosen second.
BIncorrectA restore never overwrites the existing table.
CIncorrectA stream holds only 24 hours of changes and is not a backup.
DIncorrectThe capacity mode does not recover data.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • PITR keeps 1 to 35 days, and a restore creates a new table. The same is true for on-demand backups.
  • Export to S3 needs PITR and uses no capacity. Import creates a new table.
  • Encryption at rest is always on in DynamoDB.
  • Private subnet must reach DynamoDB without a NAT gateway or the internet = gateway VPC endpoint. From on-premises over Direct Connect or VPN = interface endpoint.
  • Each user may access only their own items = IAM condition dynamodb:LeadingKeys, often with Cognito identity pools.

Memory Hook

PITR = any second, up to 35 days. Export = analytics in S3, no capacity.

Trigger 1: "Recover a table to a specific second"
→ Point-in-time recovery

Trigger 2: "Query DynamoDB data with Athena without using table capacity"
→ Export to Amazon S3

Trigger 3: "Copy DynamoDB backups to another Region"
→ AWS Backup

Trigger 4: "Lambda in a private subnet calls DynamoDB without NAT or internet"
→ Gateway VPC endpoint for DynamoDB

Trigger 5: "Reach DynamoDB privately from on-premises"
→ Interface VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink)

Trigger 6: "Users may only access their own items"
→ dynamodb:LeadingKeys in the IAM policy

6. DynamoDB Pricing

Problem Statement

The FlashCart bill lists reads, writes, storage, backups, and replicated writes. The CFO asks what drives each line, and which choices are safe to change to lower the total without hurting the shop.

6.1 What You Pay For

Prices change often and differ by Region. Check the current rates on the Amazon DynamoDB pricing page, and estimate your own cost with the AWS Pricing Calculator.

  • Reads and writes: request units on demand, or the provisioned RCUs and WCUs.
  • Storage: a price per GB-month for the table data and the indexes. Standard-IA lowers it.
  • Replicated writes: a global table is billed for the writes that DynamoDB replicates to every replica Region.
  • Backups: PITR is charged by the size of the table, including the local secondary indexes, and on-demand backups by their size.
  • DAX: the nodes of the cluster, per hour.
  • Streams and data transfer: read requests of streams, and data that leaves AWS or moves between Regions.

6.2 Lowering the Cost

  • Use provisioned capacity with auto scaling for steady traffic, and on-demand for spikes.
  • Use reserved capacity for a steady provisioned workload, where it is available for your table class.
  • Use Standard-IA for large tables that are read rarely.
  • Use TTL to delete expired items for free, so that the storage stays small.
  • Project only the attributes that you need into a GSI.
  • Use Query and not Scan, and keep the items small.

6.3 Exam-Style Question

Written for this course.

Scenario: A DynamoDB table has steady, predictable traffic all day, and the company is paying on-demand prices. The company wants to lower the cost. Which solution meets the requirements?

  • A. Switch the table to provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling.
  • B. Keep on-demand mode and add DAX.
  • C. Switch to Standard-IA for a table that is read all day.
  • D. Turn on global tables.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: A. Provisioned capacity is cheaper per request for steady traffic, and auto scaling handles small changes.

OptionResultReason
ACorrectIt lowers the cost for a steady workload.
BIncorrectDAX adds a cost, and it helps only repeated reads.
CIncorrectStandard-IA raises the request cost for a frequently read table.
DIncorrectGlobal tables add replica and replicated write charges.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • Choosing on-demand for steady traffic costs more. Choosing provisioned for spiky traffic can throttle.
  • Global tables add the storage and the replicated writes of every replica Region.
  • TTL deletions are free. PITR is billed by table size.

Memory Hook

Steady = provisioned. TTL = free delete. Global tables = pay for every replica.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "Lower the cost of a steady DynamoDB workload"
→ Provisioned capacity with auto scaling and reserved capacity

Trigger 2: "Lower the storage cost of a rarely read table"
→ Standard-IA table class

Trigger 3: "Remove old items with no write cost"
→ TTL

7. Comparison & Scenarios

7.1 DynamoDB Compared With Other Databases

DynamoDBRDS and AuroraDocumentDBElastiCache
ModelKey-value and document (NoSQL).Relational (SQL).Document (MongoDB-compatible).In-memory key-value cache.
ScalingServerless, automatic.Instance sizing and replicas.Instances and replicas.Nodes and shards.
Joins and ad hoc SQLNo.Yes.No joins like SQL, rich queries on documents.No.
LatencySingle-digit milliseconds, microseconds with DAX.Milliseconds.Milliseconds.Sub-millisecond.
Best forKnown access patterns at any scale.Joins, transactions, and ad hoc queries.MongoDB workloads.Caches and sessions.

7.2 DAX Compared With ElastiCache

DAXElastiCache
SourceOnly DynamoDB.Any database, API, or computation.
Code changeSmall: the client and the endpoint.Your code must read, write, and invalidate the cache.
What it cachesIndividual objects, and the results of Query and Scan.Individual objects, and aggregation results.
FeaturesItem and query cache.Rich data structures, such as sorted sets, pub/sub, and streams.
Choose it whenThe source is DynamoDB and the reads repeat.The source is RDS or Aurora, you need advanced features, or one cache serves many systems.

7.3 DynamoDB in Serverless Architectures

  • A serverless REST API: clients call Amazon API Gateway (lesson 273.2) over HTTPS, API Gateway invokes AWS Lambda, and Lambda reads and writes DynamoDB. Amazon Cognito authenticates the users, and a DAX cluster in front of the table adds a caching layer for read-heavy, static data.
  • Row-level security: Cognito identity pools can exchange a login token for temporary AWS credentials, and an IAM policy can restrict each user to their own items in a DynamoDB table.
  • Event-driven flows: a DynamoDB stream invokes a Lambda function when an item is created, and the function, with an IAM role, uses Amazon SES to send a welcome email.
  • Global reach: a global table serves the REST API data with low latency in several Regions. Aurora Global Database could serve read-only data, but it has one writer Region.

Placing an order is a write, and Aurora Global Database has read replicas in the other Regions, but only one writer Region.

7.5 Choosing Cost-Effective Database Services

A cost-effective database is one that fits three things: the access pattern (steady, spiky, or idle), the query needs (lookups by key, or joins and ad hoc queries), and the operations that your team wants to avoid. The cheapest service on paper is not cost-effective if it does not fit the workload. Prices change often, so check the pricing pages and the AWS Pricing Calculator before you decide.

7.5.1 What Drives the Cost of Each Service

ServiceThe main cost driversNote
Amazon RDSDB instance hours (by engine and class), storage and Provisioned IOPS, the Multi-AZ standby, each read replica, backups beyond the free amount, and data transfer.You pay for the instance while it runs, even when it is idle. A stopped instance still pays for storage, and RDS restarts it after 7 days.
Amazon AuroraInstance hours, or ACU-hours for Serverless v2, the storage that you use, and I/O requests (Standard) or no I/O charge (I/O-Optimized).Serverless v2 follows the load, and a minimum of 0 ACUs lets an idle instance pause.
Amazon DynamoDBRead and write requests (on-demand) or provisioned capacity, storage (Standard or Standard-IA), and optional features such as global tables, point-in-time recovery, and DAX.There is no instance. An idle table costs only its storage, and in on-demand mode requests cost nothing when there is no traffic.
Amazon ElastiCacheNode hours, or data stored and compute for Serverless.A cache lowers the cost of a larger database.
DocumentDB, Neptune, and KeyspacesInstance hours or serverless capacity, storage, and I/O or requests.Each has a serverless or on-demand option for variable workloads.

7.5.2 DynamoDB Compared With Amazon RDS on Cost

Amazon DynamoDBAmazon RDS
Billing basisRequests or provisioned capacity, plus storage.Instance hours, plus storage and I/O.
Idle costVery low with on-demand mode.The instance is billed all the time that it runs.
Spiky trafficOn-demand mode scales on its own, and you pay per request.You size the instance for the peak, or you add replicas, and you pay for the capacity.
Steady trafficProvisioned capacity with auto scaling, and reserved capacity, lower the cost.Reserved Instances lower the cost of a steady instance.
High availabilityData is replicated across Availability Zones by default, with no extra standby to pay for.A Multi-AZ deployment adds the cost of a standby instance.
Query flexibilityEfficient only for the access patterns that you design. A scan of a large table is slow and costly.Joins and ad hoc queries are built in, so they cost no extra design work.
Best forKnown key-based access patterns at any scale, especially with spiky traffic.Joins, ad hoc queries, and complex transactions, or an application that already uses SQL.

7.5.3 Serverless Options

  • DynamoDB on-demand mode: no capacity to set, and you pay per request.
  • Aurora Serverless v2: capacity in ACUs follows the load, and a minimum of 0 ACUs lets an idle instance pause.
  • ElastiCache Serverless: a cache with no nodes to choose.
  • Neptune Serverless and DocumentDB Serverless: graph and document capacity that follows the load.
  • Keyspaces on-demand mode: no capacity planning for Cassandra-compatible tables.
  • Serverless fits variable, unpredictable, and intermittent workloads. For a steady, high workload, provisioned capacity with a reservation is usually cheaper.

7.5.4 Ways to Lower the Database Cost

  • Match the capacity mode to the traffic: provisioned for steady, on-demand or serverless for spiky or idle.
  • Use Reserved Instances for a steady RDS or Aurora instance, and reserved capacity for a steady provisioned DynamoDB table.
  • Put a cache in front of the database: DAX for DynamoDB, and ElastiCache for RDS and Aurora, so the database needs less capacity.
  • Use DynamoDB Standard-IA and TTL for cold data, and export old data to S3.
  • Use Single-AZ and smaller or serverless databases for development and test.
  • Choose Aurora I/O-Optimized when the I/O charges are a large share of the Aurora bill.
  • Use Storage Auto Scaling with a maximum, and delete old snapshots.
  • Do not use a scan for reports. Export the data to S3 and query it with Athena.

7.7 Lesson Summary

This lesson covered the following points:

  • DynamoDB is a serverless NoSQL database. Items are identified by a partition key, or a partition key plus a sort key, and can hold up to 400 KB. Query uses the key, and Scan reads everything.
  • Provisioned mode fits steady traffic and can throttle. On-demand mode fits spikes and unknown loads. Standard-IA lowers the storage cost of cold tables.
  • A GSI adds a new access pattern at any time, and an LSI adds a sort order at table creation. Reads can be eventually consistent, strongly consistent, or transactional.
  • Global tables are multi-active across Regions. DAX caches reads in microseconds. Streams keep 24 hours of changes. TTL deletes expired items for free.
  • PITR restores to any second in 1 to 35 days as a new table. Export to S3 supports analytics with no capacity use. Encryption at rest is always on.
  • A cost-effective choice matches the access pattern: DynamoDB on-demand mode or Aurora Serverless v2 for spiky and idle workloads, and provisioned capacity or Reserved Instances for steady ones. A cache lowers the cost of the database behind it.

Memory Hook

Partition key places it. Global tables write anywhere. DAX reads in microseconds. Streams tell the world. TTL cleans for free.

8. Knowledge Check

Answer each question in your own words before you open the model answer. The questions were written for this course.

Question 1: Explain how a DynamoDB table identifies an item, and the difference between Query and Scan.

Maps to: Objectives 1 and 2 (Comprehension).

Each item is identified by its primary key, which is a partition key alone or a partition key plus a sort key. DynamoDB uses the partition key to place the item. Query finds items by the partition key and optional sort key conditions, and reads only the matching partition. Scan reads every item in the table or index, even when you add a filter, so it is slow and costly on large tables.

Question 2: Compare provisioned and on-demand capacity modes, and say how many capacity units a strongly consistent read of a 10 KB item takes.

Maps to: Objective 3 (Analysis).

Provisioned mode needs you to set RCUs and WCUs, is cheaper for steady traffic, and can throttle on a spike. On-demand mode scales by itself, fits unpredictable traffic, and costs more per request. One RCU covers a strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB per second, so a 10 KB item takes 3 RCUs.

Question 3: Explain when to use a global secondary index and when to use a local secondary index.

Maps to: Objective 4 (Application).

A GSI has a different partition key, can be added at any time, has its own capacity, and offers eventually consistent reads. Use it for a new access pattern, such as lookups by product. An LSI keeps the table partition key with a different sort key, must be created with the table, uses the table capacity, and also supports strongly consistent reads.

Question 4: Describe DynamoDB global tables, DAX, Streams, and TTL, and what each one solves.

Maps to: Objective 5 (Comprehension).

Global tables replicate a table across Regions with multi-active reads and writes, for low latency and Regional resilience. DAX is an in-memory cache that serves repeated eventually consistent reads in microseconds. Streams record item changes for 24 hours to trigger Lambda or other consumers. TTL deletes expired items in the background at no write cost.

Question 5: Explain how to recover a DynamoDB table, and how to analyze its data without using its capacity.

Maps to: Objective 6 (Application).

Point-in-time recovery restores the table to any second in the recovery period of 1 to 35 days, and on-demand backups restore to the time of the backup. A restore always creates a new table. To analyze the data, export the table to Amazon S3 from a PITR point, which uses no read capacity, and query it with Athena.

Question 6: Design the data layer for a global shopping site that needs millisecond reads, writes in three Regions, a cache for hot products, and low cost for old orders.

Maps to: Objective 7 (Synthesis).

Use a DynamoDB global table with replicas in three Regions for active-active writes and local reads. Choose provisioned mode with auto scaling for the steady base and on-demand for a spiky table. Put a DAX cluster in front of the hot product reads. Move the old orders table to the Standard-IA class, use TTL for expired sessions, turn on PITR, and export history to S3 for analytics.

Question 7: Describe a serverless architecture with DynamoDB for a mobile app that needs authentication, fast repeated reads, and a welcome email for each new user.

Maps to: Objective 5 (Application).

The mobile client authenticates with Amazon Cognito and calls Amazon API Gateway over HTTPS. API Gateway invokes AWS Lambda, which reads and writes the DynamoDB table. A DAX cluster between Lambda and the table caches the repeated reads in microseconds. When a new user item is created, DynamoDB Streams invoke a second Lambda function, which has an IAM role and uses Amazon SES to send the welcome email. A global table can serve the same data in several Regions.

Question 8: Describe the data types and the naming rules of DynamoDB, and explain how you store a date.

Maps to: Objectives 1 and 2 (Comprehension).

DynamoDB has scalar types (number, string, binary, Boolean, and null), document types (list and map, nested up to 32 levels), and set types (string set, number set, and binary set, with unique values of one type and no empty sets). The key attributes must be a string, a number, or binary, and the other attributes are not defined in advance. Names are UTF-8 and case-sensitive. Table and index names are 3 to 255 characters and use only letters, digits, underscores, dashes, and dots. Attribute names should be short, because they count in the metering. DynamoDB has no native date type, so you store a date as an ISO 8601 string or as an epoch number, and you use epoch seconds for TTL.

Question 9: Compare a relational database such as Aurora with DynamoDB, and say when you choose each one.

Maps to: Objectives 1 and 2 (Analysis).

A relational database such as Aurora has a defined schema, uses SQL with joins and ad hoc queries, supports ACID transactions, and scales up and by replicas, with a limit on the size. DynamoDB is schemaless apart from the primary key, is accessed by key with secondary indexes, scales out with no limit on the table size, and gives steady millisecond performance at any scale. Choose a relational database for joins, ad hoc queries, and complex transactions. Choose DynamoDB for web-scale workloads with known access patterns and a flexible schema.

Question 10: Choose cost-effective database services for three workloads: a spiky key-value workload, a steady relational workload that will run for three years, and an idle development database.

Maps to: Objective 8 (Evaluation).

For the spiky key-value workload, use DynamoDB in on-demand capacity mode, because there is no idle capacity and you pay per request. For the steady relational workload, use RDS or Aurora with Reserved Instances, because a reservation lowers the price of an instance that runs all the time. For the idle development database, use Aurora Serverless v2 with a minimum of 0 ACUs, so that the instance pauses and does not bill for compute while it is idle. A cache such as DAX or ElastiCache can lower the capacity that the database needs.

Question 11: A flash sale causes throttling on one product key while the table has spare capacity, two shoppers sometimes buy the same last unit, and a Lambda function in a private subnet calls DynamoDB through a costly NAT gateway. Explain the cause and the fix of each problem.

Maps to: Objectives 2 and 6 (Analysis).

The throttling is a hot partition: one partition key receives more than the partition limit of 3,000 read units or 1,000 write units per second, so extra table capacity does not help. Spread the load with a high-cardinality key or write sharding, and cache hot reads with DAX. The double sale is a lost update: use a conditional write with a version attribute, or a condition that stock is greater than zero, so only one write succeeds. The NAT cost is avoidable: add a gateway VPC endpoint for DynamoDB, which keeps the traffic private with no hourly charge.
